title: Shock = delivery failure
body: Shock is inadequate perfusion, not a BP number.
Pump fails → cardiogenic. Pipes too wide → distributive. Fluid lost → hypovolemic.
Something squeezing or blocking the pump → obstructive.
On any scenario, ask: which part of the system broke?

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: The plumbing math
body: CO = HR × SV
BP = CO × SVR
Pulse pressure = SBP − DBP
MAP ≈ DBP + ⅓ pulse pressure
Stroke volume depends on preload, contractility, and afterload.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: Why BP lies
body: Baroreceptors trigger a sympathetic surge: faster rate, stronger squeeze, vasoconstriction.
Hormones (RAAS, ADH) hold onto fluid; blood is shunted from skin and gut to core organs.
The body can hide about 25% volume loss behind a normal BP.
Early signs: tachycardia, anxiety. BP drops late, often past 30% loss.
Best brain-perfusion indicator: level of consciousness.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: Cellular collapse
body: No oxygen → anaerobic metabolism → lactic acid.
ATP runs out → the sodium/potassium pump fails → cells swell and self-digest.
Acid and CO₂ buildup dilate vessels, undoing compensation.
End state: multiple-organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS), often hours to days later.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: Telling the types apart
body: Hypovolemic: cool, pale, clammy · tachycardic · flat neck veins.
Cardiogenic: cool, clammy · brady or tachy · JVD.
Obstructive: cool, clammy · tachycardic · JVD.
Distributive: usually warm · rate varies · flat neck veins.
Discriminators: skin temperature, then neck veins plus lung sounds.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: Distributive subtypes
body: Septic: infection; skin often warm or hot despite shock.
Neurogenic: spinal injury; hypotension WITHOUT tachycardia, warm dry skin below the injury.
Anaphylactic: vasodilation plus bronchospasm; epinephrine is the only reversing treatment.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: Obstructive subtypes
body: Tamponade: Beck's triad = JVD, muffled heart tones, narrowing pulse pressure.
Tension pneumo: needs needle decompression; tracheal deviation is late. Be careful with positive pressure.
PE: 250 mL bolus, recheck BP, repeat if SBP stays under 90.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: Three stages
body: Compensated: BP held, pulse pressure narrowing, up to ~25% loss. Usually recoverable.
Decompensated: BP falling, >30% loss. Sometimes recoverable.
Irreversible: terminal.
You can't tell decompensated from irreversible in the field, so treat everyone aggressively.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: Management sequence
body: Control life-threatening bleeding first, then airway and oxygen.
Position of comfort (usually supine), vitals with SpO₂ and glucose.
IV/IO access, keep them warm with blankets (no external heat sources), nothing by mouth.
Aim for 10 minutes or less on scene; treat en route.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: Fluid rules
body: Adult hypovolemic: 20–30 mL/kg in 250 mL increments until radial pulses return.
Uncontrolled bleeding: permissive hypotension, just enough to keep a radial pulse.
Pediatric: 20 mL/kg warmed isotonic crystalloid, reassess, repeat.
Cardiogenic / tension pneumo: TKO only. Fluid overloads a failing pump.
Pregnancy: left lateral position; treat the mother aggressively to perfuse the fetus.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

conflicts.nremt: 20–30 mL/kg in 250 mL increments until radial pulses return
conflicts.ri: LR 500 mL to SBP ≥90–100 or MAP ≥65; penetrating torso without TBI: 250 mL to a radial pulse; max 2 L
LR 20 mL/kg (10 mL/kg under 3 months), max 60 mL/kg

title: Exam traps
body: Normal BP does not rule out shock.
Bradycardia + hypotension: think cardiogenic or neurogenic, then check skin temp.
Don't wait for late signs (tracheal deviation, cyanosis).
Check SBP and get IV access before nitro in any possible cardiogenic patient.
Elderly hypertensive patients can be in shock with SBP above 100.
RI 4.01A: SBP <110 in a patient over 65 may already be shock.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: Shock fluids, RI protocol detail
body: Shock = SBP <90, MAP <65, or shock index (HR ÷ SBP) ≥0.6.
General shock (2.20A): LR 500 mL, repeat to SBP ≥100 or MAP ≥65.
External hemorrhage (2.21A): control the bleeding first, then LR 500 mL to SBP ≥90 or MAP ≥65, max 2 L.
Penetrating torso, no TBI: LR 250 mL, repeat only to a radial pulse, SBP ~80, or normal mentation, max 2 L.
Penetrating torso with TBI: LR 250–500 mL to SBP ≥90 (the brain needs pressure).
Peds (2.20P/2.21P): LR 20 mL/kg (10 mL/kg under 3 months), max 60 mL/kg.
Peds hypotension: SBP <70 + (2 × age in years).

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026)

title: Conduction pathway
body: SA node → atria → AV node (built-in delay) → bundle of His → right/left bundle branches → Purkinje fibers.
Backup pacemakers get slower the lower you go: SA 60–100, AV junction 40–60, ventricles 20–40 per minute.
Cell properties: automaticity (fires on its own), excitability, conductivity, contractility.
Think of it as a relay race: if a runner drops out, the next one down takes over, just slower.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

title: Reading the paper
body: Small box = 0.04 s. Large box (5 small) = 0.20 s. 5 large boxes = 1 s; 30 large boxes = 6 s.
6-second strip: count QRS complexes × 10 (works for irregular rhythms).
Regular rhythms: 1,500 ÷ small boxes between R waves, or 300 ÷ large boxes (300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50).

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

title: Normal values
body: P wave: rounded, upright, about 2 small boxes tall or less; one before every QRS.
PR interval: 0.12–0.20 s (3–5 small boxes).
QRS: 0.04–0.12 s in this text; wider means the impulse came from, or spread abnormally through, the ventricles.
QT: normally less than half the R-to-R interval.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

conflicts.nremt: Adult texts: wide = 0.12 s or more
conflicts.ri: AHA 2025 PALS uses >0.09 s as wide in children (not an RI difference, a peds one)

title: Reading a strip, same order every time
body: 1. P waves: present? upright? one per QRS?
2. PR interval: measure each one; constant, long, or changing?
3. QRS: narrow or wide? same shape?
4. Rhythm: march out R-to-R and P-to-P (calipers or paper-and-dots).
5. Rate: atrial (P) and ventricular (R); both should match the pulse.
Then look at the patient. Treat the patient, not the monitor.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

title: Artifact
body: Static that mimics rhythms: loose or dried electrodes, patient movement, shivering, seizures, electrical interference.
Fix: dry and prep skin, fresh electrodes, still the patient, check cables.
Never call VF or asystole from the screen alone: check the patient and the leads.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

title: Sinus rhythms
body: All share: upright P before each QRS, PR 0.12–0.20, narrow QRS.
Normal sinus: 60–100, regular.
Sinus bradycardia: under 60. Sinus tachycardia: 101–150 in this text (look for a cause: pain, fever, hypovolemia).
Sinus arrhythmia: rate speeds and slows with breathing; normal in the young.
Sinus arrest/pause: a whole P-QRS-T goes missing; the next beat may come from a new site.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

title: Atrial rhythms
body: PAC: early beat with a differently shaped P wave.
SVT: regular, narrow, 151–250 in this text; P waves often hidden in the T wave; starts and stops abruptly.
Atrial fibrillation: no P waves, wavy baseline, irregularly irregular. Over 100 = rapid ventricular response.
Atrial flutter: sawtooth flutter waves; described by ratio (2:1, 3:1, 4:1) or variable.
Wandering atrial pacemaker: 3 or more P-wave shapes, rate under 100 (MAT if faster).

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

title: Junctional rhythms
body: P wave inverted before the QRS, buried in it, or retrograde after it; PR under 0.12 s if you can see it.
Junctional escape: 40–60. Accelerated junctional: 61–100. Junctional tachycardia: 101–150.
PJC: early beat with a junctional-looking P wave.
Analogy: the backup generator (AV junction) kicked in because the main power (SA node) failed.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

title: AV blocks
body: 1st degree: PR over 0.20 s, constant, every P conducted. A delay, not a block.
2nd degree type I (Wenckebach): PR gets longer, longer, longer, then a QRS drops. Pattern repeats.
2nd degree type II: PR stays the same, then a QRS suddenly drops. Can progress to 3rd degree: dangerous.
3rd degree (complete): P waves and QRS complexes march independently; PR is random. Escape is junctional (narrow, 40–60) or ventricular (wide, 20–40).
Analogy: the AV node is a doorman. 1st = slow doorman; type I = gets tired then skips one; type II = randomly slams the door; 3rd = door locked, two separate parties.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

title: Bundle branch block
body: Supraventricular rhythm (P waves present) with a wide QRS (0.12 s or more).
Often an R-S-R' (rabbit ears) shape; a 12-lead (V1, V6) tells right from left.
A new LBBB with chest pain is treated as a possible STEMI and evaluated in context.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

title: Ventricular rhythms
body: PVC: early, wide (>0.12 s), bizarre QRS with no P; T wave points the other way. Patterns: bigeminy, trigeminy, couplets, multifocal, R-on-T.
V-tach: 3 or more ventricular beats in a row, wide and fast; monomorphic or polymorphic; may or may not have a pulse.
Torsades de pointes: polymorphic VT that twists around the baseline; linked to long QT.
V-fib: chaotic, no QRS, no pulse. Defibrillate.
Idioventricular 20–40 (accelerated 41–100); agonal under 20.
Asystole: flat line. Confirm in a second lead and check leads/gain before calling it.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

title: Pulseless electrical activity
body: Any organized rhythm on the monitor with no palpable pulse.
Treat as cardiac arrest: CPR and epinephrine, and hunt for reversible causes (Hs and Ts).

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

conflicts.ri: RI 3.03A: 1 mg every 5 min, max 5 doses for non-shockable rhythms

title: Pacemakers and implanted defibrillators
body: Pacer spikes: vertical lines before the P (atrial), QRS (ventricular), or both (dual chamber).
Failure to capture: spike with no complex after it. Failure to sense: spikes fire at the wrong time.
ICD: may shock the patient on its own; you can touch them safely during CPR.
Don't place defibrillator pads directly over an implanted device.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

title: 12-lead: where's the infarct?
body: Inferior (II, III, aVF): usually the RCA. Get a right-sided lead (V4R) to check for RV infarct.
Septal (V1–V2) and anterior (V3–V4): LAD.
Lateral (I, aVL, V5–V6): circumflex.
Posterior: ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R waves.
STEMI: ST elevation in 2 or more contiguous leads (V2–V3: ≥2 mm men, ≥1.5 mm women; ≥1 mm elsewhere).

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

conflicts.nremt: Textbook: use nitro cautiously with RV involvement
conflicts.ri: RI 3.02: no nitro in RV infarction; if hypotension follows nitro, stop it and give fluid

title: Treating the big rhythms
body: Unstable = hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest pain, or acute heart failure.
Unstable tachycardia: synchronized cardioversion. Unstable bradycardia: atropine, then pacing or pressors.
Stable regular narrow tachycardia: vagal maneuvers, then adenosine.
Pulseless VF/VT: defibrillate; epinephrine and amiodarone or lidocaine.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

conflicts.nremt: AHA: 6 mg rapid IV push with flush, then 12 mg
conflicts.ri: RI 3.06A: 12 mg first, may repeat × 1

conflicts.nremt: AHA: 1 mg every 3–5 min, max 3 mg
conflicts.ri: RI 3.05A: 0.5–1 mg every 3–5 min to HR >60, max 3 mg
RI 3.06A: diltiazem only after medical control; max 20 mg first dose

title: Who counts as a child
body: Infant: under about 1 year (newborns follow neonatal guidelines). Child: 1 year to puberty. Puberty onward: adult BLS.
Kids rarely arrest from the heart itself: it's usually respiratory failure or shock first, so fix breathing early.

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 6: Pediatric Basic Life Support

title: High-quality pediatric CPR (2025)
body: Rate 100–120/min; depth at least ⅓ of the chest (about 1.5 in infants, 2 in children); full recoil.
Pauses under 10 s; pulse check no longer than 10 s.
No advanced airway: 30:2 with one rescuer, 15:2 with two (before puberty).
Advanced airway: continuous compressions, 1 breath every 2–3 s (20–30/min).
Breathing inadequately but has a pulse: 1 breath every 2–3 s; reassess pulse every 2 min.

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 6: Pediatric Basic Life Support

conflicts.nremt: 15:2 with two rescuers until an advanced airway is placed
conflicts.ri: RI 3.03P: continuous compressions prioritized; ventilate 20–30/min, avoid over-ventilation

title: Hand technique (changed in 2025)
body: Infants: heel of 1 hand on the sternum, or 2 thumbs with hands encircling the chest.
The 2-finger technique was removed: it rarely reached proper depth.
Children: 1 or 2 hands, whichever gets the depth.

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 6: Pediatric Basic Life Support

title: Choking (changed in 2025)
body: Mild (coughing, making sounds): let them cough and watch.
Infant, severe: 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts (heel of hand). No abdominal thrusts.
Child, severe: 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, repeated.
Goes unresponsive: start CPR with compressions, no pulse check; look in the mouth before breaths. No blind finger sweeps.

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 6: Pediatric Basic Life Support

conflicts.nremt: AHA 2025: alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts
conflicts.ri: RI 7.02: abdominal thrusts (Heimlich) only

title: Defibrillation in kids
body: AED on a child under 8: use a pediatric attenuator/pads. None available? An adult AED is still better than no shock.
Manual: 2 J/kg first, 4 J/kg second, then ≥4 J/kg up to 10 J/kg or the adult dose.
Pads: largest that fit with 1–2 cm between them; front-back or front-side both OK.
One shock, then straight back to compressions.

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 8: Pediatric Advanced Life Support

conflicts.ri: RI 3.03P matches: 2 → 4 → ≥4 J/kg (max 10 J/kg or adult dose)

title: Pediatric arrest drugs
body: Epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg (0.1 mg/mL = 0.1 mL/kg), max 1 mg, every 3–5 min. Non-shockable: give it as early as possible.
Shock-refractory VF/pVT: amiodarone 5 mg/kg (max 300 mg), up to 3 doses (max 150 mg after the first), or lidocaine 1 mg/kg.
No routine sodium bicarbonate or calcium (except special cases like hyperkalemia or sodium-channel blocker overdose).
Reversible causes: the Hs and Ts.

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 8: Pediatric Advanced Life Support

conflicts.nremt: 5 mg/kg, max 300 mg first, 150 mg after, up to 3 doses
conflicts.ri: RI 3.03P: 5 mg/kg, may repeat × 2 (no cap stated)
RI 3.03P: 1 mg/kg (max 100 mg), may repeat × 1 in 10 min

title: Pediatric bradycardia
body: Bradycardia with poor perfusion often means arrest is coming.
Oxygenate and ventilate first. HR under 60 with poor perfusion despite that: start CPR.
Epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg (max 1 mg). Atropine 0.02 mg/kg (min 0.1 mg, max single 0.5 mg, may repeat once) for vagal cause or AV block.
Consider pacing.

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 8: Pediatric Advanced Life Support

conflicts.nremt: 0.02 mg/kg, min 0.1, max 0.5 mg, repeat once
conflicts.ri: RI 3.05P matches

title: Pediatric tachycardia
body: Probable sinus tach: P waves present, variable R-R, infant under 220, child under 180. Treat the cause.
Probable SVT: no normal P waves, fixed R-R, infant ≥220, child ≥180, abrupt start.
Narrow = 0.09 s or less. Stable SVT: vagal maneuvers, then adenosine 0.1 mg/kg (max 6 mg), then 0.2 mg/kg (max 12 mg).
Unstable: adenosine if IV is ready, or synchronized cardioversion 0.5–1 J/kg, then 2 J/kg.
Wide and unstable: cardioversion; get expert consultation before more drugs.

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 8: Pediatric Advanced Life Support

conflicts.ri: RI 3.06P: 0.2 mg/kg (max 12 mg), may repeat × 1; AEMT-C needs medical control
RI 3.06P/3.07P: 1 J/kg, then 2 J/kg
RI 3.07P: amiodarone 5 mg/kg (max 150 mg) over 20 min, or lidocaine 1 mg/kg

title: Pediatric shock fluids
body: Isotonic crystalloid; balanced (LR) or normal saline both acceptable.
Septic shock: 10 or 20 mL/kg boluses with reassessment after each.
Stop for signs of fluid overload (crackles, liver enlargement, worsening breathing).

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 8: Pediatric Advanced Life Support

conflicts.ri: RI 2.20P/2.22P: LR 20 mL/kg (10 mL/kg under 3 months), max 60 mL/kg

title: Angina vs heart attack
body: ACS covers any symptoms of acute myocardial ischemia: angina and MI are treated alike in the field.
Angina: brief, predictable (stable) or not (unstable), eases with rest or nitro.
AMI: any time, lasts longer than minutes, may not ease with rest or nitro.
Women, diabetics, and older adults often present atypically: weakness, nausea, dyspnea, fatigue.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 18: Cardiovascular Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Chest pain care
body: Position of comfort; oxygen only as needed (SpO₂ ≥94%).
12-lead within 10 minutes of contact; IV access without delaying transport.
Aspirin chewed; nitroglycerin if no contraindications.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 18: Cardiovascular Emergencies (lecture slides)

conflicts.ri: RI 3.02: 81 mg × 4 (324 mg) chewed

conflicts.nremt: Textbook: SBP >90 (Ch 14) or >100 (Ch 18, heart failure); expect either on the exam
conflicts.ri: RI 3.02: SBP >100 always
RI 3.02: transmit the 12-lead, scene time ≤10 min, CODE STEMI notification

title: Cardiogenic shock
body: The pump can't push enough blood, usually after an MI.
Clues vs hypovolemic shock: chest pain, JVD, crackles, dysrhythmias, peripheral edema.
Position of comfort, oxygen to SpO₂ >94%, IV at TKO, keep warm, early ALS.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 18: Cardiovascular Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Heart failure
body: Left-sided: fluid backs into the lungs: dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, pink frothy sputum.
Right-sided: fluid backs into the body: JVD, pedal and dependent edema.
Sit them up, legs down; oxygen; CPAP; nitro if SBP >100; bring their meds.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 18: Cardiovascular Emergencies (lecture slides)

conflicts.nremt: Not an AEMT skill in most national curricula
conflicts.ri: RI 3.01: CPAP and nitro first; furosemide is second-tier (transport ≥30 min, patient already on it, SBP ≥100, max 80 mg)

title: Hypertensive emergency
body: SBP over 180, DBP 120 or higher, or a rapid rise, with signs of organ damage (headache, confusion, chest pain).
Head elevated, IV access, rapid transport.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 18: Cardiovascular Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Aortic dissection
body: Sudden tearing pain in the chest or between the shoulder blades.
Check BP in both arms; a big difference supports dissection.
Main cause: uncontrolled hypertension. Rapid transport.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 18: Cardiovascular Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Cardiac devices
body: Pacemaker and ICD: palpable bump under the skin, usually upper chest.
Wearable defibrillator vest: can shock on its own; follow its voice prompts.
LVAD: continuous flow, so the patient may have no palpable pulse; follow RI 3.08 and the device team's instructions.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 18: Cardiovascular Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Adult cardiac arrest
body: Push hard and fast, full recoil, minimal interruptions.
AED as soon as available; no touching during analysis or shock; back to compressions right after.
Remove medication patches; don't shock in pooled water; shave a hairy chest if pads won't stick.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 18: Cardiovascular Emergencies (lecture slides)

conflicts.nremt: AHA: 30:2 without an advanced airway; with one, 1 breath every 6 s
conflicts.ri: RI 3.03A: continuous compressions; for VF/VT, passive oxygenation (NRB or BVM) for the first 4 cycles, then 10 breaths/min; advanced airway only after cycle 4
RI: rhythm-check pauses ≤5 s; pre-charge the defibrillator at 1:45 of each 2-min cycle
RI: every 5 min; max 5 doses non-shockable, 3 shockable

title: IV solutions
body: Isotonic (same as blood): normal saline, lactated Ringer's. Used for volume replacement.
Hypotonic (D5W): water moves into cells.
Hypertonic (3% saline, blood products, albumin): pulls water into the vessels.
Analogy: tonicity is water chasing salt.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 13: Vascular Access and Medication Administration (lecture slides)

title: Administration sets and drip math
body: Microdrip: 60 gtt/mL (small volumes, kids, medications). Macrodrip: 10–15 gtt/mL (volume).
gtt/min = (mL × drip factor) ÷ minutes.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 13: Vascular Access and Medication Administration (lecture slides)

title: Catheter size
body: Gauge: the bigger the number, the smaller the catheter.
Large bore (14–18) for trauma and volume; 20–24 for kids, older adults, and fragile veins.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 13: Vascular Access and Medication Administration (lecture slides)

title: IV complications
body: Infiltration: swelling, cool pale skin, slowed flow. Stop, remove, restart in the other arm.
Thrombophlebitis: red, warm, tender vein. Stop and restart elsewhere.
Air embolism, catheter shear, arterial puncture, vasovagal reaction.
Circulatory overload: crackles, JVD, dyspnea. Slow to TKO, sit them up, notify.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 13: Vascular Access and Medication Administration (lecture slides)

title: Intraosseous access
body: Sites: proximal tibia (find the tibial tuberosity, then about 2 cm medial), distal tibia (2–3 cm above the medial malleolus), humeral head, sternum (sternal devices).
Don't place it in a fractured bone, through infection, or in a bone already used for IO.
Complications: extravasation, compartment syndrome, dislodgement, infection.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 13: Vascular Access and Medication Administration (lecture slides)

conflicts.ri: RI AEMT scope (1.07) includes IV and IO access

title: Drug names and schedules
body: Chemical name (structure), generic name (official, lowercase), trade name (brand, capitalized).
Controlled substance schedules I–V: I = no accepted medical use, high abuse; V = lowest abuse potential.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 12: Principles of Pharmacology (lecture slides)

title: Autonomic receptors
body: Alpha-1: vasoconstriction. Beta-1: heart rate and contractility up. Beta-2: bronchodilation.
Memory hook: 1 heart, 2 lungs.
Parasympathetic (acetylcholine): slows the heart, makes secretions. Anticholinergics (atropine) block it.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 12: Principles of Pharmacology (lecture slides)

title: Routes, fastest to slowest
body: IV/IO fastest; then inhaled, intranasal, IM, subcutaneous, oral.
Absorption depends on blood flow: a shocky patient absorbs IM and SQ poorly.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 12: Principles of Pharmacology (lecture slides)

title: Key electrolytes
body: Sodium: water balance. Potassium: heart rhythm (high or low K both cause dysrhythmias).
Calcium: muscle contraction and clotting. Magnesium: nerve and muscle function.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 8: Pathophysiology (lecture slides)

title: Acid–base in one card
body: Respiratory acidosis: hypoventilation (CO₂ builds). Respiratory alkalosis: hyperventilation.
Metabolic acidosis: DKA, shock (lactic acid), overdose. Metabolic alkalosis: vomiting, antacids.
The body compensates: fast deep breathing (Kussmaul) blows off CO₂ in metabolic acidosis.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 8: Pathophysiology (lecture slides)

title: Cellular injury
body: Hypoxia is the most common cause of cell injury.
Other causes: chemicals, infection, immune reactions, genetics, nutrition, physical agents.
Unchecked shock leads to MODS: organ failures cascading hours to days later.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 8: Pathophysiology (lecture slides)

title: Medical patient approach
body: Scene size-up and standard precautions first; nature of illness from the scene and bystanders.
Responsive patient: history drives it (OPQRST, SAMPLE). Unresponsive: rapid full-body exam.
Choose the destination by capability (stroke, STEMI, trauma centers), not just distance.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 16: Medical Overview (lecture slides)

title: Infectious diseases and PPE
body: Airborne (TB, measles): N95 on you; mask the patient if tolerated.
Droplet (influenza, pertussis, meningitis): surgical mask.
Bloodborne (HIV, hepatitis B/C): gloves, eye protection; hepatitis B vaccine is available.
MRSA: contact precautions and hand hygiene.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 16: Medical Overview (lecture slides)

title: Four ways breathing fails
body: Upper airway obstruction: foreign body, trauma, inflammation (epiglottitis, croup).
Lower airway obstruction: bronchospasm, mucus, obstructive lung disease.
Chest wall impairment: trauma, pneumothorax, hemothorax, neuromuscular disease.
Neurologic control problems: brainstem injury, stroke, drugs that blunt the respiratory drive.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 17: Respiratory Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Alveoli, surfactant, and the V/Q match
body: Type I alveolar cells do the gas exchange; Type II make surfactant and new Type I cells.
Surfactant lowers surface tension so alveoli stay open; collapsed or fluid-filled alveoli can't exchange gas.
Chronic hypoxia leads the body to overproduce RBCs (polycythemia); thicker blood strains the right heart (cor pulmonale).

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 17: Respiratory Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: CO2 retention and hypoxic drive
body: Chronic CO2 retention makes the brain's CO2-sensing drive less responsive over time.
Hypoxic drive is a backup: the brain breathes based on low O2 instead of high CO2.
Heavy supplemental O2 can blunt that backup drive and depress respirations, but never withhold O2 from a patient who needs it; support ventilation instead.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 17: Respiratory Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Hypo/hyperventilation and the I:E ratio
body: Hypoventilation traps CO2 and causes respiratory acidosis.
Hyperventilation (tachypnea without a physiologic O2 demand) drops CO2 and causes respiratory alkalosis; can mimic a panic attack.
Normal expiration lasts about twice as long as inspiration (I:E ratio); prolonged in asthma, shortened in tachypnea.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 17: Respiratory Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: COPD: chronic bronchitis vs emphysema
body: Chronic bronchitis: mucus-gland overgrowth, productive cough 3+ months/year for 2+ years.
Emphysema: alveolar wall destruction from lost surfactant, irreversible; the most common form of COPD.
Acute COPD picture: pursed-lip breathing, barrel chest, tripod position, days of worsening dyspnea.
Dry lungs — pair with pulmonary edema's wet lungs for the breath-sound gut check; treat the patient, not just the sounds.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 17: Respiratory Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Asthma: the reversible triad
body: Bronchospasm plus mucus production plus airway edema: all three, and all reversible.
Status asthmaticus: a severe attack that doesn't respond to conventional treatment, a dire emergency.
A silent chest in an asthmatic isn't improvement, it's a pre-respiratory-arrest sign.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 17: Respiratory Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Pulmonary edema: wet lungs
body: Fluid floods the alveoli and lung tissue, cutting gas exchange.
Cardiogenic: left heart can't keep up with the right, back-pressure floods into the lungs.
Noncardiogenic causes: smoke/toxic fume inhalation, chest trauma, high-altitude exposure.
Classic picture: dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, crackles.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 17: Respiratory Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Pneumothorax vs pleural effusion
body: Spontaneous pneumothorax: air in the pleural space; tall thin young males at higher risk.
Sharp pleuritic pain, unilaterally decreased/absent breath sounds, local hyperresonance to percussion; tracheal deviation is a late sign.
Pleural effusion: fluid outside the lung; decreased breath sounds over the fluid, dull to percussion, patient usually feels better sitting upright.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 17: Respiratory Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Pulmonary embolism
body: A clot (usually from a leg or pelvic vein) lodges in a pulmonary artery and blocks blood flow, a V/Q mismatch.
Risk factors: immobilization, recent surgery, pregnancy, prior PE, obesity, oral contraceptives, cancer, long-distance travel, sickle cell disease.
Signs: sudden dyspnea, tachycardia, tachypnea, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia, sometimes hemoptysis.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 17: Respiratory Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Croup vs epiglottitis vs bronchiolitis
body: Bronchiolitis: under 2 y/o (peak 3-6 mo), viral (RSV), wheeze/crackles, gradual onset, largely supportive care.
Croup: 6 mo-6 y/o, viral, barking cough plus stridor, gradual onset with cold symptoms.
Epiglottitis: usually over 2 y/o, bacterial, sudden onset, toxic-appearing, drooling, tripod; avoid airway manipulation and suctioning.
Always consider a foreign body first in a child who went from eating to short of breath.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 17: Respiratory Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Naming abnormal breath sounds
body: Crackles (rales): fine, crackling, air moving through fluid in the alveoli.
Rhonchi: lower-pitched, secretions/mucus in the larger airways.
Stridor: high-pitched, inspiratory, upper-airway obstruction.
Wheezing: high-pitched, typically expiratory, bronchoconstriction/inflammation.
Pleural friction rub: squeaking/grating, inflamed pleural linings rubbing together.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 17: Respiratory Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Oxygen targets and CPAP
body: Target SpO2 94-99%; avoid pushing to 100%.
CPAP: for patients not improving on nebulizer therapy, or in cardiogenic pulmonary edema; raises intrathoracic pressure.
CPAP risk: can drop preload/BP in a hypotensive patient, and can convert a simple pneumothorax into a tension pneumothorax.
CPAP tends to succeed if the patient's own respiratory rate starts to fall after application, and tends to fail if it keeps climbing.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 17: Respiratory Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Glucose, insulin, and glucagon in one card
body: Glucose is the brain's only fuel; without it, brain cells are damaged fast.
Insulin (beta cells) lets glucose into cells everywhere except the brain, which doesn't need it.
Glucagon (alpha cells) raises blood glucose by triggering the liver to break down glycogen (glycogenolysis).

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Hypoglycemia vs DKA vs HHNS at a glance
body: Onset: hypoglycemia is minutes; DKA is hours to days; HHNS is days to weeks.
Skin: hypoglycemia is pale/moist; DKA and HHNS are warm/dry.
Breath: DKA has a fruity/acetone odor from ketones; HHNS does not (no ketosis).
Glucose: hypoglycemia under 60 mg/dL; DKA usually over 250 mg/dL; HHNS often over 600 mg/dL.
Kussmaul respirations (deep, rapid) belong to DKA, blowing off CO2 to fight the acidosis.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: DKA and HHNS aren't the same failure
body: DKA: usually type 1, no insulin at all, fat gets burned for fuel, ketones build up into metabolic acidosis.
HHNS: usually type 2, some insulin is still around, enough to prevent ketosis, but glucose and dehydration climb much higher.
HHNS fluid deficits can run 10 L or more; give fluid more cautiously with a heart-failure or renal history.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Treating low glucose, by route
body: Alert, can swallow safely: oral glucose (tablets, gel, juice, non-diet soda, sugar); don't be shy with the amount.
Altered or can't protect the airway: nothing by mouth; go IV dextrose, or IM/IN glucagon if there's no IV access.
Glucagon only works if the liver has glycogen stores to draw from; pair it with dextrose when you can.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Sickle cell crisis: five patterns
body: Vaso-occlusive: sickled cells jam small vessels causing pain, ischemia, organ damage; the most common presentation.
Acute chest syndrome: a vaso-occlusive crisis with fever, chest pain, hypoxia, cough; treat as a lung emergency too.
Aplastic crisis: bone marrow shuts down, worsens baseline anemia; pallor, tachycardia, fatigue.
Hemolytic crisis: RBCs break down faster than normal, hemoglobin drops fast.
Splenic sequestration: painful, sudden spleen enlargement; hard, bloated abdomen.
Pulse oximetry can be unreliable in sickle cell crisis.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Clotting gone two ways
body: Hemophilia A (low factor VIII) and B (low factor IX): genetic, same signs, bleeding takes longer to stop.
Thrombophilia: an increased tendency to clot; recent surgery, immobility, cancer, pregnancy, smoking, long travel all raise risk.
DIC: clotting factors get consumed treating a triggering illness, then flip to uncontrolled bleeding; high mortality.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Anemia in the field
body: Low hemoglobin/RBC count cuts the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.
Presents as fatigue, weakness, and sometimes angina-type chest pain from reduced O2 delivery to the heart.
Iron-deficiency anemia is the most common type; causes range from bleeding to autoimmune RBC destruction.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Adrenal insufficiency: the hidden shock
body: Suspect it with a history of Addison's disease, HIV/AIDS, or chronic (even recently stopped) steroid use.
Hypotension that resists IV fluids or pressors is the classic tell.
The adrenal glands can't mount a stress-cortisol response; illness, trauma, or burns can tip a borderline patient into crisis.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Blood, in four jobs and three organs
body: Plasma carries everything; RBCs carry oxygen; WBCs fight infection; platelets start clots.
Bone marrow makes blood cells; the liver makes clotting factors and filters blood; the spleen filters and recycles RBCs.
ABO plus Rh typing is why mismatched transfusions can cause rapid, severe reactions.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

title: Reading the patient before the glucometer
body: Warm, dry skin plus Kussmaul respirations plus fruity breath points to hyperglycemia/DKA.
Moist, pale skin plus rapid weak pulse plus normal-to-rapid shallow breathing points to hypoglycemia.
Never assume altered mental status is just a known diabetic's baseline; check a blood glucose every time.
Sickle cell clues on scene: swelling of fingers/toes, jaundice, priapism, pain isolated vs. whole-body.
